❯ Write a 3000-word short story about a lighthouse keeper, in plain prose. End with the line THE END.

● The Last Watch at Gannet Rock

  The letter reached Gannet Rock in March, folded inside a brown envelope with the harbour authority's crest in the
  corner. Walter Dunning read it twice at the kitchen table. It said that the station would be decommissioned at the end
  of the navigation season, that the optic would be removed to a museum in the city, that his long service was deeply
  appreciated, and that a pension review would follow in due course. He folded it along its creases and slid it under
  the sugar bowl, where it stayed for three days.

  He was sixty-eight. He had been keeper of the Gannet Rock light for thirty-one years, and for the last eleven of them
  he had been keeper of very little. The lamp had been automated in the year his daughter turned seventeen. Since then
  the light turned by itself, the fog signal sounded when the sensor said fog, and the radio beacon sent its
  identification every thirty seconds whether anyone was listening or not. Walter's job had become a list of checks. He
  walked the gallery each morning and read the gauges. He wrote the log. He cleaned the lens on Thursdays, though it
  hardly needed it, because the new lamp was sealed and the salt air could not get at it the way it used to.

  On the fourth morning after the letter, he took it out from under the sugar bowl, read it once more, and went up the
  tower to do the checks.

  The stairs were a hundred and twelve steps of cast iron, painted white so many times that the paint had a soft,
  rounded look at the edges. Walter counted them out of habit. He had counted them in the first week, carrying his
  wife's suitcase up with one hand and holding his daughter against his shoulder with the other, and he had counted them
  every day since, though he could no longer remember why he started. At the top the lamp room was warm from the lamp,
  and the glass of the lantern threw the morning back at him in pieces.

  From the gallery he could see the whole of the sea. On clear days you could make out the mainland as a low grey line,
  and the harbour lights at the far end of it, and in the evenings the lights of the ferry coming and going. Today there
